opus-5.5.text:
I think the core intuition is that the physical world doesn't come to us in separate channels. When you watch someone pour water into a glass, you see the motion, you hear the pitch of the sound rising as the glass fills, and if you're the one pouring, you feel the weight shifting in your hand and adjust your wrist. All of that is one event. Splitting it into a video model, an audio model, a language model, and a policy model is an engineering convenience, not a reflection of how the world actually works.

So when we train these modalities together, each one becomes a kind of supervision signal for the others. Video gives you very dense information about geometry, motion, and cause and effect, but it's ambiguous: from pixels alone, it's hard to tell whether an object is heavy or light, or what someone intends to do. Language is the opposite. It's very sparse, but it carries abstraction, intent, and common sense, the "why" behind what you're seeing. Audio is underrated, I think. It tells you about material properties, contact, collisions, things that are often occluded or invisible in the frame. And action is what grounds everything. If a model has to actually predict what a robot or an agent should do next, it can't just produce something that looks plausible. It has to be consistent with physics and with the goal.

What we've seen, and what motivates this direction, is that a shared representation trained on all of these tends to be more physically grounded than one trained on any single modality. Action data is expensive and scarce, but video is abundant, so the model can learn a lot of world dynamics from video and transfer that to action. Conversely, the small amount of action data acts as a strong constraint that pulls the video predictions toward things that are physically realizable rather than just visually pleasing. Language then lets you steer and query all of this in a way humans can work with.

I'd also say it's about generalization. If you want a model that can be dropped into a new environment and reason about what will happen, it needs a holistic understanding, not a collection of narrow skills stitched together. Bringing language, video, audio, and action into one model is our bet that a unified world model will be more capable than the sum of its parts. We're still early, and there's a lot we don't understand yet about how to balance the modalities, but the signal so far has been encouraging.

r001.rationale: It says action prediction grounds the model in physics and goals, but does not state that jointly predicting the observation resulting from an action improves action learning.

r002.rationale: It says audio can reveal contact and collisions, but does not explain that an impact sound identifies the moment of contact in generated video.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute text-to-video difficulty to the many possible videos matching a text description.

r004.rationale: It does not state that more detailed text descriptions make good video generation easier.

r005.rationale: It acknowledges that modalities need balancing, but does not identify adjusting training-data proportions as a way to make them complement one another.

r006.rationale: It grounds cross-modal complementarity in the idea that the modalities describe one event and that the physical world does not come in separate channels.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The intuition is pretty simple when you think about how humans learn. A child doesn't learn about the world through one channel. They see things move, they hear the sound it makes, they reach out and touch it, and eventually someone names it for them. Those signals arrive together, and they constrain each other. Language alone can't tell you how a glass shatters. Video alone can't tell you why someone dropped it.

So when we built Cosmos 3, we wanted a single model where each modality fills in what the others can't express well. Video carries the physics, the geometry, how objects move and deform over time. Language carries abstraction and intent, the reasons behind what's happening and the ability to generalize across situations that look very different on the surface. Audio carries timing and causality that's often invisible, a motor straining, a collision happening off screen. And action is the bridge to the physical world. It's what lets a robot or an autonomous vehicle actually do something, and it's the modality that's most scarce in data.

That scarcity is really the key argument. There are relatively few hours of robot demonstration data in the world compared to the enormous amount of video and text. If you train on action alone, you're starving the model. But if the model has already learned from video how the world evolves, and from language what people are trying to accomplish, then the action data only has to teach the last mile, mapping that understanding onto motor commands. We see this empirically. Pretraining on video and language makes the policy learn faster and transfer better to new environments.

It also goes the other direction, which people sometimes miss. Action data improves the video model. When the model knows what command was issued, it learns that the outcome in the next frame isn't random, it's caused. That makes the world model more physically grounded instead of just producing plausible-looking pixels. And language grounding lets you ask the world model counterfactual questions. What happens if I push this box harder? That's reasoning, not just prediction.

So the short version is that each modality has a blind spot, and the others cover it. A unified representation lets the abundant data subsidize the scarce data, and it lets the model reason about the physical world in a way that no single modality could support on its own. That's what we mean when we say they help one another.

r001.rationale: The response says action data can improve the video model and that video-language pretraining helps policies learn faster, but it does not state that jointly predicting the observation resulting from an action improves action learning.

r002.rationale: It says audio can reveal an off-screen collision, but does not say an impact sound identifies the contact moment in generated video.

r003.rationale: The response discusses what language and video each convey, but does not attribute text-to-video difficulty to one description matching many possible videos.

r004.rationale: It does not state that adding detail to text descriptions makes video generation easier.

r005.rationale: It describes abundant modalities subsidizing scarce action data, but does not identify adjusting training data proportions as a way to prevent modalities from interfering.

r006.rationale: The response says the modalities arrive together and constrain one another, then explains how they each describe aspects of the physical world, grounding complementarity in their shared world.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that these modalities describe different aspects of the same world. Video shows you what is happening, audio gives you information you may not see, language helps express intent, and action connects what you do to what happens next.

For example, imagine a robot picking up a cup. Language specifies the goal. Video helps locate the cup and observe its motion. Sound might tell you whether contact occurred. And the action provides context for predicting what the robot should observe next. Each modality can help resolve ambiguity in the others.

If we learn those relationships together, the model can potentially develop a more coherent understanding of the world. That is the motivation for combining them in Cosmos 3: better understanding can support better action, and learning the consequences of actions can improve understanding.

r001.rationale: It says action provides context for predicting what the robot observes next, but does not state that jointly predicting action outcomes improves action learning in world action models.

r002.rationale: It says sound might indicate whether contact occurred, but does not explain that an impact sound identifies the moment of contact in generated video.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the difficulty of text-to-video generation or the many videos that can match a text description.

r004.rationale: It does not state that adding detail to text descriptions makes video generation easier.

r005.rationale: It does not mention adjusting training data proportions to encourage modalities to complement rather than interfere with one another.

r006.rationale: It explicitly grounds the intuition in the modalities describing different aspects of the same world.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that these modalities describe different aspects of the same world. Video shows you what is happening, audio gives you information that may be difficult to see, language lets you describe intent, and action tells you how an agent interacts with its environment. When you learn them together, each provides context that can help interpret the others.

For example, imagine a robot manipulating an object. The video shows the motion, the sound can provide a clue about contact, and the action tells you what the robot did to produce that change. Language can specify the goal. Together, these signals can help the model learn a more coherent relationship between intent, action, and outcome.

That is the motivation for combining them in Cosmos 3: we want the model to use complementary information to better understand and predict what happens in the world.
